# The Lighthouse Keeper

When the autumn storms finally reached the northern coast of the island, the old lighthouse keeper climbed the long spiral stair for the last time that year, and he counted every step as he had done since he was a boy. Mr. Hale had kept the light for forty years. He knew each crack in the stone and each rattle of the glass. The sea that night was grey and heavy, and the wind carried the smell of salt and wet rope across the cliffs.

Dr. Brooks arrived from the mainland on the morning ferry. She carried a small leather bag and a letter from the harbour office. "You must be the doctor," said Mr. Hale, and he held the door against the wind. "I am," she answered. "I came as soon as I could." The two of them sat by the stove while the kettle began to sing.

The letter was short. It said that the lamp would soon be replaced by an automatic light, and that the keeper would retire at the end of the season. Mr. Hale read it twice and folded it along the old creases. He did not say anything for a long while. Then he asked about the weather on the water, because that was the only thing that mattered to him.

The tower was exactly 31.5 metres tall, and the lamp turned once every 12.5 seconds. Dr. Brooks measured the stair with a tape and wrote the numbers in a notebook. She liked numbers, and she liked the way they stayed the same when everything else changed. Pi, she said, is about 3.14, and no storm will ever alter that.

After supper they climbed to the lantern room together. The lens was as tall as a man and shone like a block of ice. Mrs. Lane, the cook, had sent up a basket of bread, cheese and apples, and they ate in silence while the beam swept the dark water. Far below, a single fishing boat was heading for the harbour.

The keeper kept a short list on the wall beside the window:

- Polish the brass every Monday.
- Check the oil before dusk.
- Write the weather in the log at midnight.

He had never missed an entry. The log filled forty shelves in the cellar, and the oldest books were written by a keeper whose name nobody remembered. Prof. Ward from the university wanted to study them, but Mr. Hale said that the books belonged to the lamp and not to the town.

By midnight the wind had grown stronger. Waves broke against the rocks with a sound like distant thunder. Dr. Brooks stood at the glass and watched the foam climb the cliff, and for a moment she felt very small. "Does it ever frighten you?" she asked. "Only when it stops," he said, and he smiled for the first time that day.

In the morning the storm was gone. The sky was pale and clean, and the gulls were back on the roof. Mr. Hale walked down to the shore and picked up a piece of green glass that the sea had polished smooth. He put it in his pocket, next to the letter, and he thought that the island would remember him longer than any machine.
